taxonomy.alias_rationale: This table used to run the other way, and CF-P7-016 turned it around. The old reasoning was that the frozen UI contract and the API contract named three failures differently and neither could be edited to match the other. That was wrong about which document was in error: the UI contract's UNAUTHENTICATED and RECENT_AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED are spellings the API catalog does not contain at all, so the map was aliasing real catalog codes onto invented ones. CF-P7-016 renamed them to AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED and REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED and mapped the whole catalog. What remains is a genuine wire join in the opposite direction: the implemented Workers handlers emit UNAUTHENTICATED and RECENT_AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED on the wire, and no Phase 7 story may change a handler. Without these two entries a real 401 or 403 from Preview would reach the unrecognised bucket and lose its unauthorized presentation. SESSION_EXPIRED no longer needs an alias because it now has a mapping of its own, and it is emitted nowhere in functions/ in any case.

availability.rationale: js/deployment.js returns available for any *.pages.dev hostname, which is true of the Production Pages deployment where COLLABORATION_ENABLED is false and no D1 exists. Before CF-P7-013 that verdict only controlled a hidden banner; the lazy opener turned it into a clickable door, so the Phase 7 boundary of no collaboration activation was in play. A hostname cannot tell an enabled Cloudflare deployment from a disabled one, so the deployment is asked directly and its COLLABORATION_UNAVAILABLE outranks the hostname. The hostname check stays as a pre-filter because it is free, runs eagerly, and is correct about GitHub Pages and unknown origins, which is where failing closed matters and where no request should be spent.

declared_limits.reason: CF-P7-015 built the layer the surfaces were always meant to call and wired the session through it, which is what moved the entry off a permanent loading state; two of the ten journey surfaces were reachable from the entry when it shipped, and the other eight were declared here rather than left to be discovered. CF-P7-013 closed that limit: it composed the eight into the panel and fed each one from its own authorized read through this client. The split is no longer taken on trust either -- the gate now walks the entry's import graph and refuses a surface claimed reachable that nothing imported renders, and one claimed pending that the entry already reaches.

sign_in_wiring.reason: Discovered live against the rebuilt Preview deployment (91e68f21, commit 42a9bee): the composed unauthorized state rendered a 'Sign in with GitHub' control with data-collab-action="sign-in", but nothing in js/collaboration/ ever listened for a click on it -- the exact 'missing a CSRF-exempt path through the API client' limit CF-P7-013 had already declared, now closed rather than left recorded.
sign_in_wiring.fix: js/collaboration/api-client.js gained beginSignIn(), the one function permitted to send a mutation before a session is resolved and without a CSRF token -- POST /api/v1/oauth/github/transactions with purpose 'sign_in' is the one mutation the frozen server contract (functions/_lib/identity/request-policy.ts) accepts unauthenticated. Every other mutation is unaffected: mutate() still refuses without a resolved session and a live CSRF token. js/collaboration/entry.js gained bindSignIn(), delegated on the shell container in the same pattern as the workspace switcher, which calls it and navigates the browser to the returned authorizationUrl.
sign_in_wiring.reauthenticate_not_exempted: purpose 'reauthenticate' is not offered through beginSignIn and is not exempt server-side; it must go through mutate() like any other mutation, with the CSRF token an existing session already holds.
sign_in_wiring.verified_live: Confirmed against the real Preview deployment: POST /api/v1/oauth/github/transactions with purpose sign_in returned 201 with a valid GitHub authorizationUrl, 3/3 attempts, after the CSRF-exempt path was added. The click itself was verified structurally (a simulated click on the rendered control redirects to the returned URL; a refused attempt shows its own reason and does not navigate; a second click while the control is disabled is ignored) rather than against the live deployment, which requires entering GitHub credentials no agent may supply.
sign_in_wiring.regression_found_and_fixed: The first version of beginSignIn() called interpret(), which reads envelope.data -- correct for every other route, but functions/_lib/identity/runtime-handler.ts answers this one route with {authorizationUrl, expiresAt} at the top level, predating the {data, meta} envelope. That mismatch parsed as ok:true, data:null and crashed the caller with "Cannot read properties of null (reading authorizationUrl)" -- found live, by clicking the real button on the rebuilt Preview deployment, not by a test, because every fixture the original suite used also assumed the wrong (enveloped) shape. beginSignIn() now parses this route's real success shape directly; a REGRESSION test in tests/collaboration-api-client.test.mjs asserts an enveloped body is rejected rather than silently read as success.
sign_in_wiring.second_regression_found_and_fixed: A far more severe instance of the same defect class was in resolveSession() itself, discovered live: after CF-P7-017 and the beginSignIn fix landed, the user completed a real GitHub sign-in, a valid unexpired session was confirmed server-side (read-only D1 check), and the composed UI still showed the sign-in prompt. GET /api/v1/session answers {authenticated, user, session, csrfToken} directly, the same unenveloped shape as the transactions route, and resolveSession() read result.data (always null for this route) unconditionally reporting authenticated: false regardless of what the server actually said. Every fixture in this suite, in collaboration-entry.test.mjs, collaboration-integration.test.mjs, collaboration-services.test.mjs, and in the live CF-P7-013 gate (scripts/cloudflare-phase-7-preview-policy.mjs) used the same wrong (enveloped) shape, which is why the signed-in path had never actually been exercised against a real deployment before this session. Both routes now share readUnwrappedIdentityResponse(); a REGRESSION test proves an enveloped session response reports authenticated: false rather than true.
